claims.text: Facebook use predicts moment-to-moment declines in affective well-being over time.
Facebook use over a two-week period predicts declines in overall life satisfaction over time.
Direct social interaction predicts increases in affective well-being over time.
Direct social interaction does not predict changes in cognitive life satisfaction.
Baseline affect levels do not predict subsequent changes in Facebook usage.
Loneliness predicts subsequent increases in Facebook usage over time.
Direct social interaction magnifies the negative effect of Facebook use on affective well-being.
Individual difference variables such as network size, perceived support, gender, self-esteem, depression, and motivation do not moderate Facebook's impact on well-being declines.

evidence.description: Nested time-lag analyses indicated that the more people used Facebook the worse they subsequently felt, B = .08, x2 = 28.90, p < .0001.
Average Facebook use over the 14-day period predicted life satisfaction declines at the end of the study, B = -.012, b = -.124, t(73) = -2.39, p = .02.
Direct social interaction predicted increases in affective well-being, B = -.15, x2 = 65.30, p < .0001.
Direct social interaction did not predict changes in cognitive well-being, B = -.006, b = -.059, t(73) = 1.04, p = .30.
The reverse pathway (T1 Affect predicting T1–2 Facebook use, controlling for T0–1 Facebook use) was not significant, B = -.005, x2 = .05, p = .82.
Loneliness significantly predicted changes in Facebook use over time, B = .07, x2 = 8.54, p < .01.
Facebook use and direct social contact interacted significantly to predict changes in affective well-being, B = .002, x2 = 19.55, p < .0001.

In no case did Facebook friend count, network support, depressive symptoms, loneliness, gender, self-esteem, or motivation interact significantly with Facebook use to predict well-being changes (ps > .16).

methodologies.name: Experience-sampling methodology
methodologies.description: Text-messaged 82 participants 5 times per day over 14 days to measure real-time Facebook use, affect, worry, loneliness, and direct social interaction, paired with pre- and post-study life satisfaction surveys.
conditions: 5 text-message prompts per day within 168-minute random windows

limitations.text: Previous research relied on cross-sectional designs, making it impossible to determine causal temporal ordering.
The sample was concentrated on young adults, so findings may not generalize to other age demographics or other social network platforms.
The observed statistical effect sizes of Facebook usage on well-being were relatively small.
Affect was measured using a single bipolar scale, which can obscure whether outcomes specifically reflect reductions in positive affect, increases in negative affect, or both.

future_work.text: Examine whether findings generalize to broader age groups and other online social networks.
Investigate underlying mechanisms such as social comparison or interference with physical activity.
Conduct experimental studies manipulating Facebook use in daily life to establish definitive causal relations.
Administer two unipolar affect questions to measure positive and negative affect separately.
